entries.meaning: Having consoled everyone in this way, Rāma joyfully bowed his head to his teacher's lotus feet, invoked Gaṇeśa, Gaurī, and Śiva, received their blessing, and set out. At his departure the grief was extreme; the city's anguished cry cannot be borne in the telling. Ayodhyā was filled with ominous signs and sorrow, while even heaven stood helpless between joy and grief. When the king recovered from his faint, he called Sumantra and asked how life could remain in his body when Rāma had gone to the forest. What pain could be stronger than one that makes a sufferer abandon body and breath? Regaining composure, the king told his friend to take a chariot and accompany them. The two princes and Janaka's daughter were very delicate; Sumantra should seat them in the chariot, show them the forest, and return after four days.

If the two steadfast, truth-bound brothers would not return, the king continued, Sumantra should fold his hands and persuade the princess of Mithilā to come back. Once she had seen the frightening forest, he should deliver the timely message that both her parents-in-law had asked their daughter to return. She might stay sometimes in her father's house and sometimes with her in-laws, wherever she preferred. Sumantra must attempt every means, for if she returned she would be a support for his life; otherwise death was his certain end, though hostile Fate had now left nothing in his control. Having spoken, the king fainted and fell to the ground, crying for Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sītā to be brought back. Receiving the royal order, Sumantra bowed, swiftly prepared the chariot, and drove outside the city to where Sītā and the two brothers waited.

Sumantra repeated the king's words, respectfully seated Rāma in the chariot, and set out with Sītā and both brothers. Riding away, they bowed inwardly to Ayodhyā. When the people saw Rāma depart and Ayodhyā left orphaned, all followed in anguish. The ocean of compassion urged them back in many ways; compelled by love they turned, only to follow again. Ayodhyā appeared terrifying, like a dark night of death. Its men and women looked at one another as though each were a dreadful beast; houses seemed cremation grounds, relatives ghosts, and sons, friends, and well-wishers messengers of Yama. Trees and vines in the gardens withered, and no one could bear to look at rivers or ponds. Horses, elephants, multitudes of pleasure animals and city cattle, together with chātakas, peacocks, cuckoos, cakravākas, parrots, mynas, cranes, swans, and cakoras all shared the desolation.

Everyone stood distraught at separation from Rāma, as motionless as figures drawn in a picture. The city that had flourished became a dreadful wilderness, crowded only with birds and beasts—that is, all its men and women. Fate had made Kaikeyī a huntress who set an unbearable forest fire in all ten directions. Unable to endure separation from Raghu's champion, every person ran after him in distress. They resolved within that without Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sītā there could be no happiness: wherever Rāma was, the whole community would be, and Ayodhyā had no purpose without Raghu's hero. Firm in this counsel, they left homes containing pleasures hard even for gods to obtain. How could sense enjoyments bind those who loved the lotus feet of Rāma? Leaving children, elders, and houses behind, the people all followed; on the first day Raghunātha camped on the bank of the Tamasā.

Seeing the people mastered by love, compassionate Rāma felt their pain especially, for the merciful lord quickly perceives another's suffering. He spoke tenderly and affectionately, explaining in many ways and offering abundant instruction in dharma, yet their love would not allow them to turn back. Rāma was caught in a dilemma because he could not abandon either gracious conduct or affection. Worn by sorrow and fatigue, the people fell asleep, their understanding somewhat clouded by divine Māyā. When two watches of night had passed, Rāma lovingly told Sumantra to drive the chariot along confusing tracks; no other method would resolve the matter. Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sītā mounted after bowing to Śiva's feet, and the minister at once drove this way and that, hiding the trail.

At dawn everyone awoke, and a great cry rose when they found Raghunātha gone. They could discover the chariot's track nowhere and ran through the four directions calling Rāma's name. They resembled a great merchant company whose ship had sunk in the ocean. Each advised another, saying Rāma had abandoned them because he knew their weakness. They condemned themselves and praised the fish: shame on life without Raghu's hero! If Fate had ordained separation from their beloved, why had it not granted death when they asked? Lamenting in countless ways, they returned to Ayodhyā filled with torment. Their fierce separation cannot be described; only hope in the fixed term kept them alive. Men and women began disciplines and vows for the sake of seeing Rāma, like cakravāka birds and lotuses left wretched without the sun.

words: the foe of darkness, the sun

entries.meaning: Sītā, Sumantra, and the two brothers reached Śṛṅgaverapura. Rāma descended, saw the divine river, prostrated, and felt exceptional joy. Lakṣmaṇa, Sumantra, and Sītā also bowed; with all of them present, Rāma found happiness. The Gaṅgā is the source of every joy and auspicious blessing, the maker of every happiness and remover of every pain. Recalling innumerable sacred accounts, Rāma gazed upon her waves and explained to the minister, his younger brother, and his beloved the abundant glory of the heavenly river. They bathed, the fatigue of the road departed, and they drank her pure water with glad hearts. Since remembering her removes the burden of toil, any fatigue here belongs only to the ordinary pattern of human conduct: the pure, conscious, blissful source of the solar line was acting out a human life as a bridge across the ocean of worldly existence.

When Guha, king of the Niṣādas, received the news, he rejoiced, summoned his dear kinsmen, loaded baskets with fruit and roots as offerings, and set out with immeasurable gladness. He prostrated, laid the gifts before Rāma, and gazed on his lord with deep love. Rāma, naturally overcome with affection, asked after his welfare and seated him nearby. Guha replied that seeing his lord's lotus feet made him fortunate and well. The earth, wealth, home, and realm were Rāma's; Guha was only a lowly servant with his family. He begged Rāma to honor the city with his feet and establish his people, so all would envy his fortune. Rāma answered that everything he said was true, wise friend, but his father's command had brought him there: for fourteen years he must dwell in the woods on a sage's vow, in ascetic dress and diet, so residence in a village was not proper. Hearing this, Guha felt a heavy grief.

Looking at Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sītā, the village men and women lovingly wondered what kind of parents could have sent such children into the forest. Others said the king had done well, since Fate had thereby given their eyes this reward. The Niṣāda chief considered within and chose a charming śiṃśapā tree; taking Raghunātha there, he showed him the place, which Rāma found delightful in every way. After the townspeople paid homage and returned home, Rāma went to perform the evening observance. Guha prepared and spread a clean, soft bed of kuśa grass and fresh leaves, and filled leaf-cups again and again with pure, tender, sweet fruit, roots, and water. Sītā, Sumantra, and the brothers ate; then the jewel of Raghu's line lay down while his younger brother massaged his feet.

Knowing his lord slept, Lakṣmaṇa rose, gently told Sumantra to sleep, and sat some distance away in the warrior's posture with bow strung and arrows ready. Guha summoned trustworthy watchmen and stationed them with great care at every place; then he himself sat by Lakṣmaṇa, quiver at his waist and bow and arrow prepared. Looking upon the sleeping lord, the Niṣāda was overcome by love and grief. His body thrilled, tears flowed from his eyes, and he spoke lovingly to Lakṣmaṇa: the king's naturally beautiful palace found no equal even in Indra's dwelling. Its lovely jeweled upper rooms seemed fashioned by the god of love with his own hands. There were pure, richly varied pleasures, flowers, fragrance, perfume, charming beds, jeweled lamps, and every kind of comfort.
